name: Backhand block
summary: Angle the bat, meet the ball early in front of the body, and let the ball's speed do the work.
whenToUse: Against loops and fast topspin to your backhand, especially when you are close to the table.

keyPoints.stance: Square to the table, knees bent, weight forward.
keyPoints.bodyAction: Almost none. Keep the head still and the body facing the ball.
keyPoints.strokeLength: A few centimetres forward. No backswing.
keyPoints.timing: On the rise, just after the bounce.
keyPoints.tablePosition: Close: half a metre from the end line.
keyPoints.batArm: Elbow in front, bat in front of the stomach, face closed over the ball.
keyPoints.recovery: Reset the bat to the middle at once.
keyPoints.anticipation: Heavy loop = more closed; fast flat drive = more open and firmer.

cues: Bat in front of your stomach
Angle over the ball, no swing

learningPath.task: Watch the block from the front. See how small the movement is.
learningPath.passCheck: You can say the three cues.

learningPath.task: Follow-along: bat in front, tiny forward push, reset.
learningPath.passCheck: 3 sets of 10, then yes to all self-checks.
selfChecks: Did the bat stay in front of your stomach?
Was the face closed over the ball?

learningPath.task: Block slow topspin to your backhand. Find the angle.
Block a steady loop until 15 in a row.
Test: backhand blocks in a row.

gamePatterns.situation: Your opponent opens with a loop to your backhand.
gamePatterns.how: Block wide to their forehand, then be ready for a wide ball to your backhand.
Soft block short over the net: they have to run in.

causes: Grip too tight against a fast ball
fixes: Close the face more over the ball
Soften the grip to absorb speed

troubleshooting.symptom: The ball goes into the net
causes: Face too closed for a light ball
fixes: Step in and take it on the rise

troubleshooting.symptom: It feels like the ball hits me
causes: Bat beside the body instead of in front
fixes: Bat in front of your stomach
Elbow forward and a little out

penholdNotes: Traditional penhold blocks on the forehand face with the wrist turned in; modern penholders can block on the reverse side like shakehand players.
